Tariffs: Washington and Beijing discuss a mutual cut on $30bn of goods each, ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting

On Friday, November 13, Americans and Chinese held the first video meeting of their new trade council, announced on Saturday by Beijing. On the agenda: a reciprocal tariff cut on $30bn of goods on each side and farm purchases, just days before a Trump-Xi summit [1][2][3].
China's Commerce Ministry described the talks as “frank, in-depth and constructive,” without saying whether an agreement had been reached [1][2].
The talks covered a mechanism for reciprocal tariff cuts on $30bn of each country's goods, farm trade and other issues of mutual concern [1][2].
This trade council was agreed in May, at the summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Beijing, then fleshed out in Washington in September [2].
The planned package, worth $60bn in total, would include about $17bn of US farm products, the equivalent of what China imported in 2024. It is not yet finalized [4].
On the US side, the Trade Representative (USTR) is setting up a bilateral “board of trade” for non-sensitive goods, while warning that “substantial” tariffs will remain in place [5].
According to the White House, the two leaders will meet on Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China [2].

Key takeaway: the world's two largest economies are trying to ease their trade war in small packages rather than through one big deal. A mutual cut on $30bn each is modest, but it can serve as a sign of détente before Thursday's summit [1][2][4].
For Donald Trump, farming is also at stake: American farmers depend on Chinese purchases, and the package under discussion includes about $17bn of farm products [4].

The White House has less room to maneuver: in February 2026, the Supreme Court struck down tariffs based on an economic emergency law (IEEPA), forcing the administration to use other legal grounds [6]. And since the Democrats' victory in the midterms, its trade policy faces more pushback in Congress [6].
Nothing is settled: Beijing has announced no concrete result, and Washington insists on keeping high tariffs [2][5].

A détente between Washington and Beijing reassures global markets, and therefore European companies heavily exposed to China, such as luxury goods or carmakers. But if the Chinese buy more American soybeans and farm products, European exporters, including French farmers, could lose market share in China.

France: a fifth Saturday of anger over the cost of living, 106,000 protesters according to the state, 200,000 according to unions, as the movement loses steam

On Saturday, November 14, for the fifth Saturday in a row, marches were held across France against the high cost of living and for young people. The Interior Ministry counted 106,000 protesters, including 24,000 in Paris, compared with 146,000 the week before. Unions claim 200,000 and are preparing a strike on Tuesday [1][3][4].
According to the Interior Ministry, 106,000 people protested in France, including 24,000 in Paris. A week earlier, it had counted 146,000 [3][4].
The youth union coalition claims 200,000 protesters, including 100,000 in the capital, compared with 250,000 the previous Saturday by its own count [3][5].
As on the three previous Saturdays, about 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed. By 6 p.m., the ministry had recorded 219 arrests, fewer than in previous weeks [1][3].
Tensions flared in several cities: burning barricades in Lyon, clashes with police armored vehicles in Bordeaux, according to footage from France 24 [2].

Protesters denounce the cost of living, the state of public services, the lack of funding for schools, child protection measures and a new police bill that its opponents call a “license to kill” [1][2].
Unions rejected the 0.6% minimum wage increase promised by the government as insufficient, and are calling for a new day of strikes on Tuesday, November 17 [1].
The mood is tense for the executive: according to recent polls, Emmanuel Macron's popularity has fallen to its lowest level since he took office at the Élysée in 2017 [1].

Key takeaway: social anger is not going away, but it is weakening in the streets. Between Saturday, November 7 and Saturday, November 14, the police saw the number of protesters fall by about 27%, and the unions by 20%. The movement is entering a phase where it needs to find a second wind [3][4][5].

For Sébastien Lecornu's government, the decline is a relative relief. It does not solve the underlying problem: the demands are about purchasing power, at a time when the 2027 budget is looking for savings in public services and the minimum wage is rising by only 0.6% [1][2].
The movement is also changing shape. It is no longer just about Saturdays: it now relies on weekday strikes, like Tuesday's, which weigh more heavily on the economy and public services [1].

Finally, the protest goes beyond the economy: the police bill and violence at the end of marches are fueling a debate on law enforcement, which the government must handle without stoking tensions [1][2].

On Tuesday, November 17, expect disruptions in schools, government offices and possibly transport. As for your wallet, the 0.6% minimum wage increase is still the only measure announced: if you are paid the minimum wage (Smic), it may not make up for rising energy and food prices.

Czech Republic: Prague may see the largest protest in its history against Babiš, who wants to scrap the public TV and radio license fee

This Sunday, November 15, at 2 p.m., the association A Million Moments for Democracy is calling for a protest on Letná Plain in Prague against Prime Minister Andrej Babiš's plan to scrap the public television and radio license fee. The district town hall expects up to several hundred thousand people [1][2][3].
The rally is called “Letná against 4:36 a.m.,” a reference to the time at which the coalition pushed the bill through its first reading, in the middle of the night, on Saturday, October 24 [1][4][5].

The bill scraps the 205-koruna monthly fee (about $9.40) paid by households and funds Czech Television and Czech Radio from the state budget. Their combined budget would fall by 15% compared with this year [5].

The Prague 7 town hall expects up to several hundred thousand participants; organizers speak of the largest rally in Czech history. Volunteers have chartered 50 buses from across the country, and metro and tram services are being stepped up [2][3][6].

Organizers are demanding that the bill be withdrawn and that the government apologize for the overnight vote [3]. On November 3, 1,376 employees and freelancers at Czech Radio and 2,257 at Czech Television had already gone on strike [7].

Andrej Babiš is not backing down: the strike will change nothing, and the fee will be scrapped, he says. According to him, payments guaranteed by law and indexed to inflation will protect public media from arbitrary cuts [7][8].
His opponents argue instead that state funding will weaken these media and expose them more to political pressure [8].
The prime minister will be in Israel from November 16 to 18 and will miss the November 17 commemorations marking the anniversary of the Velvet Revolution, which the opposition criticizes [9].

Key takeaway: the license fee battle has become a test of public media independence in the Czech Republic. Its opponents see it as a disguised takeover; the Babiš government, as a simple funding reform [5][8].
The mechanism is simple: a fee paid directly by households escapes the government's spending decisions, whereas a line in the state budget can be trimmed every year by the ruling majority [5][8].

The domestic standoff adds to European tensions: Andrej Babiš and Slovakia's Robert Fico are joining forces against Berlin on aid to Ukraine, with Fico refusing to pay “a single euro” toward a new loan [10].
The bill still has to go through committee and then a second and third reading. The size of Sunday's crowd will show whether the street can force a government with a majority to back down [4][7].

The question of how to fund public broadcasting also comes up in France: the Czech debate shows what is at stake when the money goes through the state budget. And in Brussels, a Czech government at odds with the EU weighs on major decisions, such as funding for Ukraine, which French taxpayers also guarantee.

In Manila, Carney wraps up a free trade deal with the Philippines and nearly another with all of Southeast Asia, to depend less on Trump

On Saturday, November 14, in Manila, on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit, Mark Carney announced the end of negotiations on a free trade agreement between Canada and the Philippines, and the “substantial” conclusion of a second agreement with the 11 ASEAN countries. Together, they open up a market of more than 700 million people. Signing is targeted for 2027 [1][4].
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed a document officially concluding the negotiations, launched just over a year ago [4].

The text has not yet been signed: the two countries have committed to doing so in 2027 [4]. The agreement with ASEAN, the bloc of 11 Southeast Asian countries, is “substantially concluded,” but its text has not been published [1][2].
According to Ottawa, trade in goods between Canada and the Philippines reached C$3.4bn in 2025 [1]. AFP, for its part, puts it at about $2.4bn [5].
ASEAN is already Canada's fifth-largest trading partner, with more than $50bn in trade a year. Ottawa is pledging $5 million to help these countries prepare for ratification [2].
A sensitive point: pork. Manila plans to raise its tariffs on foreign pork, currently 15 to 20% for Canadian pork. Canada exported $229 million worth of it in 2025 [3].

“Countries without a free trade agreement will probably see higher tariffs,” warned Mark Carney, who says he is “fighting for this industry” [3]. The agreement does not appear to exempt Canada from a temporary ban on foreign pork imports [3].
This is the fourth free trade agreement concluded by Mark Carney since he took office, after Indonesia, the United Arab Emirates and Ecuador [4].

Key takeaway: Canada, hit by Donald Trump's tariffs, is looking for other customers. With these two agreements, it gains privileged access to Southeast Asia, a fast-growing region of more than 700 million people [1][4].

Mark Carney presents these agreements as part of a strategy: building “a dense network of reliable partners” to reduce dependence on the United States [4]. He also said trade with Washington will not return to the pre-Trump “normal” [5].

The mechanism: a free trade agreement lowers or removes tariffs between signatories, which makes exporters more competitive than rivals without a deal. But until anything is signed and ratified, nothing changes in practice [4].
The timing matters: Mark Carney moves on to the Francophonie summit in Cambodia, then the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, where he wants to keep diversifying Canada's markets [6].

Canada is doing what Europe is also trying to do: multiplying trade agreements so as not to depend on a single large market.  For you, it is a sign that global trade is reorganizing around US tariffs, with effects on prices and on jobs in export industries.

Argentina: “Yes, I am aiming for reelection,” Javier Milei launches his 2027 bid and promises to give back $500bn in taxes

On Saturday, November 14, at the Casa Rosada in Buenos Aires, Argentine President Javier Milei confirmed that he will run for reelection in October 2027. He promises to keep cutting taxes and to give $500bn back to Argentines, while a poll shows that a majority do not want a second term [1][2][5].
Javier Milei made the announcement while opening an exhibition on independence hero Manuel Belgrano at the Casa Rosada museum, during “Museum Night” [1][3].
“For those who doubt it: yes, I am aiming for reelection,” he said in the presence of his sister Karina Milei [3].
He promised to “keep cutting taxes” and, if the “base scenario” comes true, to give Argentines back $500bn, the equivalent of the country's debt [2].
He set himself a trade goal: for Argentina to trade with 90% of the world's countries by 2031 [2].
In August, he still tied his candidacy to the success of his government; that condition has disappeared [4].
The general election is scheduled for Sunday, October 24, 2027; the mandatory primaries in August are on hold [4].

According to a poll published by iProfesional, 52% of Argentines think Milei does not deserve to be reelected, and only 33% of Patricia Bullrich's voters would choose his party, La Libertad Avanza [5].

Key takeaway: a year before the vote, Javier Milei is turning his economic policy into a campaign platform. He is betting that tax cuts and trade openness will be enough to win people over, while his popularity is eroding and his camp is divided [2][4][5].

The $500bn figure is more of a slogan than a plan: Milei presents it as the amount the state would give back in tax cuts if growth follows, and equates it with the amount of public debt. Nothing details the timeline or the funding [2].

The main risk comes from his own camp. Patricia Bullrich, a former security minister turned senator, has her own ambitions. The iProfesional poll shows that some of her voters would not follow Milei [5].
The timeline remains unclear: the mandatory primaries in August 2027 may not take place, which would change how candidates are chosen [4].

Argentina is a major supplier of soybeans, beef and lithium, and a key partner in the EU-Mercosur agreement. If Milei stays in power, the free-market line and trade openness will continue, which interests European companies. If he loses, a return of the Peronists could call that openness into question. Savers holding Argentine bonds will follow this contest closely.

Samsung in talks to buy US firm Modine, a data center cooling specialist: the stock jumps nearly 29%

Samsung Electronics is negotiating to buy Modine, a US company that makes cooling systems for AI data centers, according to Bloomberg. On Friday, November 13, Modine's stock jumped nearly 29% to about $137; the company was worth $5.6bn the day before [1][4].
According to sources cited by Bloomberg, Samsung and Modine are discussing a deal that could be concluded within a few weeks [1].
Nothing is done yet: the talks could still fail, and another buyer could come forward. Samsung and Modine declined to comment [1].
On Thursday evening, Modine's stock was worth $106.10 in New York, giving it a market value of about $5.6bn [1].
On Friday, the stock gained nearly 29% to about $137, one of the biggest gains on Wall Street that day [4][5].
Wisconsin-based Modine saw its sales to data centers jump 73% in its fiscal year ended in March, to $1.1bn [7].
The company also signed a contract with one customer for more than $4bn of cooling products for 2027 to 2029 [7].
For Samsung, it would be a second purchase in this sector, after Germany's FläktGroup, bought for €1.5bn [1][6].

Key takeaway: AI does not just need chips, it also needs a lot of cooling. Servers get extremely hot, and companies that know how to cool them are worth more and more. Samsung, already a memory chip giant, wants to move into this market by buying a US specialist [1][3].

The strategy is clear. In May 2025, Samsung had already paid €1.5bn for FläktGroup, citing strong demand from data centers. Modine, with a market value of $5.6bn before the news, would be a much bigger catch [1][6].

It is a delicate moment for the sector. That same Friday, chip stocks fell on Wall Street after the resignation of Jensen Huang, the head of Nvidia. But infrastructure suppliers like Modine remain in favor, because data centers keep being built [5][7].

There is also a political dimension. A South Korean group buying a US industrial company will probably need approval from Washington's authorities, at a time when AI has become a sovereignty issue. No timeline has been given [1][3].

If you have a fund invested in US stocks or in AI, this kind of deal shows where the money is going: toward what keeps data centers running (electricity, cooling), not just toward chips. For the general public, nothing changes in the short term, but the AI race is pushing up the price of everything around it.

How it works: why a target's stock jumps even before an offer

When a company wants to buy another one listed on the stock market, it generally has to pay more than the current share price: this is the “premium,” which persuades shareholders to sell. As soon as a serious rumor comes out, like the Bloomberg article here, investors buy the target's stock to benefit from this future premium [1]. Modine's stock thus went from $106.10 on Thursday to about $137 on Friday, without any official offer [1][4]. The risk is real: if the talks fail, the stock can fall back just as quickly. That is why the rise stays below what a real offer could bring. The buyer, for its part, often sees its stock stagnate or fall, because it is going to spend a lot of money.
Precedents: Samsung and its big acquisitions
Samsung buys US company Harman, an audio and car electronics specialist, for $8bn, its biggest acquisition [6].
For eight years, Samsung makes no other acquisition of that size [6].
Samsung announces the purchase of Germany's FläktGroup, a ventilation and cooling specialist, for €1.5bn ($1.7bn), from the fund Triton [6].
It is its biggest purchase since Harman; eighteen months later, it is targeting Modine, which is worth more than three times as much [6][1].

India: inflation rises to 6.09% and the Mumbai stock market slips, but the rupee, which fell close to its record low in October, holds around 94 to the dollar

On Friday, November 13, Mumbai's Sensex lost 0.39% to 81,592 points, weighed down by oil and October inflation of 6.09%. The rupee ended around 94.2 to the dollar, far from its record low of 96.96 reached in May, after a central bank rate hike [1][2][3][4].
The Sensex lost 318.56 points (-0.39%) to 81,592.45, and the Nifty 155.05 points (-0.61%) to 25,144.30 [1].
Over the week, both indices are still up: +0.7% for the Sensex and +0.5% for the Nifty, a third straight week of gains [1].
The day's decline is attributed to oil and October inflation, published at 6.09% [1].
The rupee ended around 94.20 to the dollar, down 8 paise, weakened by a stronger dollar; the dollar index rose above 103 [2].
In October, it had fallen to 96.84, 12 paise from its record low of 96.96, hit in May 2026 [3].
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had then raised its key rate by 0.25 point to 5.50%, its first hike in nearly four years [4].
Foreign investors have sold nearly $30bn of Indian stocks this year, which weighs on the currency [4].

Key takeaway: India is paying for the war with Iran through its oil. The country imports most of its crude, so expensive oil pushes up prices and weakens the rupee. October inflation, at 6.09%, pushed the stock market down on Friday, even though the week remains positive [1][4].

The rupee is nevertheless doing better than in October. It had then fallen very close to its record low, despite the RBI's rate hike. The central bank governor had responded that markets can be “irrational” and that the rupee was perhaps “undervalued” [3][4].

To defend it, the RBI has used several tools: a special window to supply dollars to state-owned oil companies, and a limit lowered from $100 million to $5 million for bets on the currency without a real business need [4][7].

But these defenses are losing their effectiveness, according to Bloomberg. Analysts polled by Reuters in October expected the rupee to stay near its lows for three to six months, with high global interest rates and expensive oil [4][5][6].

A weak rupee makes India cheaper for European travelers and buyers (textiles, generic drugs). If you have an “India” or “emerging markets” fund, it is hit by both the stock market and the currency: a fall in the rupee reduces your return once converted into euros.

How it works: why oil pushes the rupee down

India buys most of its oil abroad, and pays for it in dollars. When oil prices rise, oil companies have to buy more dollars by selling rupees: the rupee falls. That is why the RBI created a special window that supplies them with dollars directly, without going through the market [4]. A weak rupee then makes imports even more expensive, which fuels inflation, at 6.09% in October [1]. To break this cycle, the central bank can raise its rates, which makes rupee investments more rewarding and attracts capital: it did so in October, to 5.50% [4]. But if foreign investors sell their Indian stocks, as they have this year, the pressure returns [4].

news.2026-11-15-allemagne-bundestag-pouv: Germany: the Bundestag authorizes its spies to sabotage targets abroad, a contested “reform of the century”

On Friday, November 13, German lawmakers adopted by 308 votes to 190, with 71 abstentions, a reform that expands the powers of the foreign (BND) and domestic (BfV) intelligence services. The BND will be able to carry out sabotage abroad, for example disabling enemy weapons systems [1][2].
The conservative CDU/CSU and the Social Democrats of the SPD voted in favor; the far-right AfD and the radical left Die Linke voted against, and the Greens abstained [2][3].
The BND will be able, in certain cases, to take down servers of state-backed hackers. The BfV gains the right to limited covert interventions in Germany, without physical force against people [1][2].
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt speaks of a “reform of the century”; his critics plan to take the case to the Constitutional Court [2].
Key takeaway: faced with sabotage and cyberattacks by hostile states, Germany is giving its intelligence services the means to act, not just to observe [1][2].
The bill still has to pass the Bundesrat, the chamber representing the Länder; most of it is due to take effect on December 31 [2].
France has also been targeted by cyberattacks attributed to states, such as the recent hacking of supermarket refrigerators: Germany's response could inspire the French debate on intelligence powers.
Planned entry into force of the main provisions, after passage in the Bundesrat [2].

news.2026-11-15-venezuela-pdvsa-objectif: Venezuela: oil company PDVSA targets 3 million barrels a day within ten years, nearly three times its current output

On Saturday, November 14, Venezuelan state oil company PDVSA published a roadmap targeting 3 million barrels of oil a day within about ten years, the level of the late 1990s. In October, the country produced only 1.14 million, according to OPEC [1].
PDVSA president Héctor Obregón plans to end 2026 at 1.3 million barrels a day, then reach 3 million around 2036 [1].
Oil and its derivatives brought in $15.148bn between January and November 2026, or 97.1% of oil and mining revenue, according to the government [2].
On November 9, ExxonMobil signed a preliminary agreement to study a return to Venezuela, nearly twenty years after leaving [3].
Key takeaway: the government of interim President Delcy Rodríguez is betting everything on oil and on the return of US majors to revive the economy, under Washington's watchful eye [2][3].

The goal remains very ambitious: production would have to nearly triple in ten years, even though it fell from 1.16 to 1.14 million barrels between September and October [1]. The date of the elections, meanwhile, has still not been set [4].
More Venezuelan oil on the market would eventually mean a little less pressure on pump prices, currently pushed up by the war with Iran. But it will take years.
